svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 2. The leak your kill switch cannot see
svg.desc: A four step explanation of route injection, disclosed in May 2024. The attacker controls the address assignment on the local network and includes an option that pushes additional routes to the client. The operating system installs those routes, and they are more specific than the tunnel's catch-all route, so they win. Traffic for the chosen destinations leaves through the physical interface instead of the tunnel. The tunnel remains connected and healthy throughout, so the client reports success and the connection guard has nothing to react to. A band below sets out what mitigates it: binding the tunnel to a network namespace, treating untrusted networks as hostile, and checking the routing table rather than an address lookup page.
svg.text: Figure 2: The Leak Your Kill Switch Cannot See
Disclosed in May 2024, affecting every system that follows the address assignment standard. Absent from essentially all leak guidance.

svg.text: Why this belongs at the front of a leak lesson rather than in a footnote
Every other item in Figure 1 is something you configured, or your operating system chose, or your browser decided. This one is chosen by whoever runs the network you
joined, at the moment you joined it, and it is selective: they take the destinations they want and leave the rest inside the tunnel so nothing looks wrong.
It affects every operating system that implements the standard properly. It is not a flaw in any particular product, which is why no vendor has fixed it.
What actually mitigates it, in descending order of practicality

g.text: Do not join networks you do not trust, or use cellular instead. Unsatisfying, entirely effective, and free. Lesson 6.1 already argued the untrusted network case is weaker than advertised.
Bind the tunnel into a network namespace, so applications inside it can only reach the tunnel interface and injected routes on the host are irrelevant to them. Available on Linux.
Check the routing table, not an address page. Unexpected specific routes after joining a network is the only symptom, and it takes one command to see.
On a managed network, protections at the switch stop rogue address servers, which helps an organisation and does nothing for you in a hotel.

svg.text: Note what is not on that list: no setting in your tunnel client, and no leak testing website, addresses this.
Which is the point. A leak taxonomy built from testing sites will never contain the leak that testing sites cannot see.
If you take one thing from this lesson into your own writing, take the habit of asking what a test cannot detect.
